speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while in opposition, Conservative Members criticized the Liberal Government for abusing air trips which were funded by taxpayers. The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) spoke in the House for hours on the subject. I would like to quote that Member. He said:
It is astounding that we have this kind of extravaganza from a Government preaching restraint.
That sounds familiar. We have yet to hear the Hon. Member, who now sits on the government side, complain about the fact that the Government has spent more than $496,000 in the last two months on air trips, and refuses to make public the reason for the use of these sacred instruments of travel.
This is the Government that, throughout the election campaign, misled Canadian people by promising that it would bring about changes; that it would not be abusive; that it would be an open Government, and that it would create jobs. There were 338 promises in total.
The Government has yet to prove to the people of this country that what it promised during the election campaign was not "bull roney". Happiness is never having to say you are Tory.

Mr. Speaker, the Cruise missile is tested in the Primose Lake Air Weapons Range which straddles the northwest corner of my constituency.
Recently I met with the Battlefords Association for Nuclear Disarmament. Members of that group told me they were opposed to Cruise missile testing; that they were opposed to involvement with the United States; that they were opposed to defence spending, and that they were opposed to NATO. One
member of this group explained that he supported what he called the Soviet Union's "assistance" to Afghanistan.
It is my view that Canadians strive for a truly mutual, balanced and verifiable disarmament. Our Government pursues this goal by using a moderate, conciliatory approach through the channels of diplomacy. I believe that sensible and fair Canadians, the majority of our citizens, want an honest and common sense approach. Many who protest, talk about their highly moral position. Striving for peace, by any means, is moral. No side in this debate has the exclusive claim to morality.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF HELICOPTERS ON WEST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call to the attention of the House and to the people of Canada the matter of the opening of an inquest today in Port Hardy, British Columbia. The inquest is inquiring into the deaths of five fishermen and the matter of receiving inappropriate weather information on the coast of British Columbia.
It is with some pleasure that I note the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) has looked into the matter, but I would warn the Government that it is not simply a matter of weather warning improvement. The availability of search and rescue equipment on the coast of British Columbia is such that if fishermen, or indeed any people, get into difficulty, quite often in the wintertime, during daylight hours, helicopters cannot reach them because of inappropriate deployment along the coast of British Columbia. I would also point out that Sikorski and Boeing Vertol, manufacturers of helicopters, have indicated that the entire coast of British Columbia could be covered by helicopters within one hour's flying time, for a price of $10 million.
More must be done to ensure the safety of people at sea than simply tuning-up weather forecasting and weather broadcasting. The Government must show concern in many other ways by co-ordinating and improving the resources which we already have.

January 30, 1985

Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention to the fact that the current crisis in the textile and clothing industry continues and is growing worse. Thirty-four thousand jobs have been lost in that industry over the past ten years. It is a deplorable situation if we consider that it costs in excess of $250,000 to create a job a year in that sector. Many of my constituents have told me their concerns about this, and it is imperative that the Government implement policies designed to alleviate that situation.
In August 1984, there were 39,700 workers in the textile sector, and 48,100 in the clothing and hosiery sector in Quebec. Those industries account for one out of five jobs in Quebec's manufacturing industries, including several thousand in my riding of Drummond, which goes to show that those industries are a major component of our economy.
Textile and clothing imports into Canada have reached unprecedented levels in recent years. In 1983, imports rose by 25 per cent over the previous year. This unabated growth in imports means that more than 27,000 pieces of clothing come into Canada every hour, every day. This situation is the result of inaction on the part of the Liberals who were unable to adhere to the principles of their own policies.
To remedy that situation, Mr. Speaker, I would urge the Minister responsible-
I regret to inform the Hon. Member that his allotted time has expired. The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart).

Mr. Speaker, Friday last the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) introduced Bill C-26. The purpose of that legislation is to extend to needy single persons, aged 60 to 64, one of the old age security benefits, the spouse's allowance. My first reaction is to say "Hurray"! But, unfortunately, the Government has decided to add a new criterion which unfairly discriminates against 80,000 people in Canada, most of whom are women.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure not one Member of this House, whatever his political stripe, will let the legislation pass as it is now worded. Otherwise it would be a shame. If the Bill becomes law as it now stands, every time a 62-year old lady calls at one of our constituency offices and says: "I have
been turned down!", and, being asked why, she will answer: "Simply because one day I separated from my husband."
Mr. Speaker, I am counting greatly on the support of every member in this House to have the Prime Minister amend the legislation to render it accessible to all needy single persons, and I am convinced he will do so.

Mr. Speaker, unemployment remains the first concern of our government. Unfortunately, our friends opposite do not seem as sensitive as we are to this issue. They continue to make speeches and prolong unduly the debate on the Investment Canada Bill which will enable our small businesses to expand and create jobs.
Mr. Speaker, a German industrialist told me recently that many of his fellow citizens were just waiting for more favourable Canadian legislation to be passed before coming to Canada to invest and to create some of the thousands of jobs which this country desperately needs.
Mr. Speaker, the Members opposite use the Standing Orders and the procedures of this House neither to make the debate any clearer nor to improve some of our bills intended to correct a situation which has become intolerable for Canadians, but simply to score political points with the media, perhaps to be named Official Opposition of the week, the month or the year!

subtopic: ANTI-SEMITISM FIRE BOMBING OF VANCOUVER SYNAGOGUE
ANTI-SEMITISM FIRE BOMBING OF VANCOUVER SYNAGOGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with regret that I report to this House that early on Friday, January 25, the Temple Shalom on West 10th Avenue in Vancouver was fire bombed. The synagogue was gutted, and there was $400,000 damage. Later, on Monday night, again there was an attempted fire bomb at the Schara Tzedeck funeral chapel. I am sure all Hon. Members of this House will join with me in deploring these terrible attacks.
Rabbi Philip Bregman is quoted in The Globe and Mail as saying that:
-he has hired guards in the past to watch over services during this temple's high holy days in the fall. At various times during his four and a half years at the synagogue, rocks have shattered windows, his car was vandalized twice, red paint has been poured over the front doors and over the Star of David and there have been telephoned obscenities and bomb threats.
January 30, 1985

This is not Europe, Mr. Speaker; this is not Paris; this is Canada. We thought we did not have these kinds of things happen in Canada. We have been rather smug in the past. I think we should note that anti-semitism, when we think it is dead, always seems to rear its ugly head again. On the fortieth anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, I would like to think that we Canadians, all Canadians, could liberate ourselves from this terrible problem of anti-semitism.
As long as Jews are singled out and persecuted, none of us in Canada are safe, and we should express our regrets about these terrible attacks in Vancouver.

subtopic: ANTI-SEMITISM FIRE BOMBING OF VANCOUVER SYNAGOGUE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic Provinces Trowel Trades College was recently established in Sum-merside, Prince Edward Island, as a training institution to encourage young people to take up the trowel trades and meet the needs of our Atlantic building industry.
The College came about because of the foresight and commitment of union leaders, civic officials, training institutions, and federal and provincial Governments. Some of these people are in the public gallery today, including Mr. Albert Vincent, Mr. Leo Rossiter, and Mr. Derek Key. They are here to meet with members of the Atlantic caucus. They seek the support of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and the Government of Canada, as well as of officials of provincial and municipal Governments, and union leaders, in order to continue their training courses. I urge continued public support be given for assistance to this college.

subsubtopic: INTENTION TO CANCEL OUR NATIVE LAND RADIO PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been informed of the intention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to cancel its native affairs program Our Native Land. This one half hour show, which is heard nationally on Saturday evenings, is the only radio broadcast which focuses exclusively on issues which are of concern to Indian, Inuit, and Metis peoples. The approach is one of in-depth and concentration, and it is not duplicated elsewhere.
I recall, Mr. Speaker, when the CBC, under the previous Liberal administration, cut this program from one hour to one half hour. It was a disgraceful, shocking decision at that time, and I said so. Now, Our Native Land is to be cut entirely and replaced by three native news stories per week.
CBC has once again failed to carry out its mandate to reflect the culture of the peoples of Canada. I know that the
Oral Questions
CBC is responding to government directives to reduce its expenditures. There is a lot of fat in the CBC; that cannot be denied. But, please, let us get rid of one of those unneeded vice-presidents and keep Our Native Land.

subsubtopic: SOCIAL PROGRAMS-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
In the House yesterday, the Minister of National Health and Welfare seemed unable to confirm whether the options mentioned in the Government's consultation document were government policy or not. Forty-eight cents a day more for disadvantaged Canadians is almost an insult. There is uncertainty and confusion everywhere in this country, owing to a definite lack of leadership. For months, the obvious confusion in Cabinet has been causing much concern among low-income families, senior citizens and working mothers. Only a budget can put an end to the confusion.
Could the Prime Minister persuade his Minister of Finance to put an end to this confusion by bringing down a budget as soon as possible?

Saint-Maurice.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. The Government's message to Canadians this week is: "Don't have children". It is cutting the family allowances and the child tax exemption. It is going to eliminate maternity leave under the UIC, and it has done nothing about day care.
Is the Prime Minister's Government serious about eliminating maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act? If so, how does he reconcile that with the promises he made in the televised women's debate before the election? Is he telling Canadians now that we cannot afford to support women when they leave work to have children? Is that what he is telling them?

For someone who began with such promise in the Catholic Youth Organization only a few years ago-to be indulging in such distortion today! The answer is absolutely no. We are trying to do what
January 30, 1985

we have tried to do in many other instances. I say this with affection for my hon. friend. He knows, as I do, that we are trying to help those most in need in our society.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, if that is the case, how does it benefit Canadians to muse in public about the elimination of one program when they do not know where they are going with the replacement? All it does is provide confusion and uncertainty.
The Minister of Finance mentioned the elimination of social programs. Are they also considering eliminating or changing the sickness and retirement benefits under the unemployment insurance program? Are they doing that as well?
Mr. Speaker, let me say, with the greatest sincerity and seriousness, that that sort of distortion is not becoming to the Hon. Member.
Hear, hear!

I said very clearly that we were considering taking the financing of those programs out of the unemployment insurance scheme and putting them into general revenues of the federal Government. I never talked once about making any changes in the program.
As I said in a previous answer, the reason why we are doing it is to take the load off small business that is suffering from that high front-end tax, so that it can create more jobs. I should think that the Hon. Member should be encouraging us to do that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It concerns the social spending plans of the Government. The only way to increase social spending for the poor without cutting back on programs for middle income Canadians is to increase the total going into social programs and obtain the additional revenue by changing tax policy to get more revenue from the rich. In the options proposed in the paper that was released on Monday, why was this important, specific option excluded?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I say to the Member for Oshawa that his question is very similar to those asked yesterday and to which the answer was given. The answer had two aspects. First, if we increase social spending, obviously we must get the economy producing more. I think all of us agree on that.
No.

speechtext:
That is obviously one point that has to be put forward. Any other options in terms of tax reform are budgetary, and remain with the Minister of Finance.
Oral Questions
The memorizing of a precise answer does not constitute a rational reply to the question.

I will direct my supplementary question to the Minister since the Prime Minister is not dealing with the question. He has just said that the only way of getting more revenue for social programs is to have an upswing in the economy.
There are over 8,000 Canadians currently at income levels exceeding $50,000 a year-presumably working men and women-who do not pay any income tax whatsoever. There are additional thousands of upper income Canadians who, because of their high income level, had their taxes substantially reduced when others were not, a few years ago.
Why did the Government not include among its options the possibility of giving a tax increase to these people instead of middle-income families, and redistribute that income to the poor who badly need it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I looked at the position put forward by the Hon. Member yesterday, that it was coming from middle-income Canadians. I said yesterday that, according to option one, 70 per cent of the money redistributed would be coming from families above $40,000, and it would be over 80 per cent from option two.
I studied it even further last night. For families earning over $50,000, sixty per cent of the redistributed money would come from them. That is the exact group that he says to tax more.
If he goes back to the bank janitor and the bank president, he would see that the bank janitor would gain money and the bank president would lose 65 per cent of his benefits.

Mr. Speaker, once again the Minister did not deal with the question. He neglected to note in his reply that more than one million middle-income families, earning between $30,000 and $50,000-many of which are families with two-income sources-will be paying hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost benefits that they will get-
With respect.

I will come to the question, Mr. Speaker. Why, in the expressed concern of some of the poor groups themselves, has the Minister embarked upon a program that will put the major part of the burden on middle-income Canadians and redistribute that to the poor, instead of going after those Canadians who can afford it, namely, the rich, by bringing in tax reforms now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

Mr. Speaker, I will give the Hon. Member the same answer.

January 30, 1985

He might not like the answer, but it is the correct answer. The other point I would make is that the option which he put forward has some of those very adverse effects, and now he is trying to reverse quickly and cover himself. Now he is attempting to talk about the rich.
I told him that the options provide for a 65 per cent redistribution to those at a lower income. I hope he understands when I tell him again that the options he puts forward in terms of tax reform are obviously a budgetary item.

provinces in terms of their social programs and see what arrangements could be made if either of those options became government policy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Would the Minister not agree that such an investment in our municipalities creating, it is estimated, some 75,000 jobs a year, would be a wise use of public funds, and seeing as the federal Government has reduced its contribution at the municipal level to almost nothing, would the Minister now make a commitment to meet with representatives of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to expedite an agreement which would allow work to begin this spring?

Member that, in the last couple of months, I have had the benefit of meeting with students and with unemployed young people in Regina, in St. John's, Newfoundland, in Halifax, in Toronto-all across the country-so that I could have their input with regard to the summer programs which will be forthcoming. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce to the House today the Government's policy on metric conversion. During the last few months we have had exhaustive consultations with retailers, various associations, consumers, business and many Canadians who wanted to express their views. We have reached a decision which, I believe, will satisfy the requirements and expectations of both business and individual Canadians, as well as current market requirements.
In the early seventies, as part of the planning for the conversion process, the economy was divided into more than 100 sectors. In each sector, conversion was initiated on a voluntary basis with the full co-operation of the industry and at the rate decided on by the industry. However, in the retail sectors, and more specifically with respect to gas and diesel fuel, home furnishings and individually weighed foods, it was decided to adopt regulations that would make the use of metric units compulsory and limit the use of imperial units. These regulations were adopted under the Weights and Measures Act.

Canadians feel, and we agree, that a compulsory "metric only" approach is both insensitive and heavy-handed.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Therefore, the three regulations under the Weights and Measures Act covering fuels, home furnishings and individually-measured foods will be revoked. They will be replaced with new provisions allowing the use of metric only or the use of imperial units alongside metric units in the advertising, displaying and weighing, and measuring of these groups of products. In all other sectors the situation will remain unchanged.
This means that consumers who are unfamiliar with the metric system can continue to refer to imperial measures while buying products in these three retail sectors. However, metric will continue to be required in these sectors, to ensure that consumers can easily compare prices between stores and products. This will also guarantee fair and equitable competition among retailers.

For small retailers, Mr. Speaker, abiding by the new policy entails practical difficulties, harsh consequences and undue expenditures, so they will be exempt from provisions concerning weighing and measuring. In other words, they will be allowed to continue to use imperial scales. However, they will be expected to use the metric system alone or in conjunction with the imperial system in advertising, displays and labelling.
January 30, 1985

Canadian industry and retailers have spent a lot of money to convert to the metric system. Today's young school graduates are familiar only with the metric system. We do know that the way the metric system has been forced upon retailers has been a source of problems for the many Canadians who find it difficult to use only the metric system.
The Government is committed to metrication, but the significant point is that it will achieve it through a more flexible and more humane process than has been the case so far. This new approach, which allows the use of both imperial and metric systems, takes into consideration the concerns expressed by our fellow citizens, yet it will eventually meet their basic requirements.

January 30, 1985

The House resumed from Monday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the motion of Mrs. Tardif (Charlesbourg) (p. 1708).

Mr. Speaker, I know that I have only four minutes left and that other Members are waiting anxiously for the Committee on Management and Members' Services, which I have the honour to chair, to begin its meeting. It is in the interests of Hon. Members opposite that I should leave the House to chair this meeting, especially in view of the order of business for today. It concerns several of them.
The Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif), who is Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), did me the honour of quoting something that I had said. However after thanking her for this kindly gesture yesterday and upon reflection, I went back to the source, since I am a cautious man, and saw that she had not quoted me accurately.
The Hon. Member and Parliamentary Secretary said the following:
As one of their own, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) said, the real work on a Bill does not take place in the House. Let us therefore proceed and go to committee right away.
I would not really have any objections to that going down in history as something I said, but this is only her interpretation of what I said. My comments were as follows, as reported on page 1636 of Hansard for January 24, 1985:
I often think we can be more effective through our work in parliamentary committees, in caucus, and by travelling across the country-
I want to make it quite clear that I was not contradicting myself and did not say that we should proceed and go to committee right away since so few of the Hon. Member's colleagues had taken part in the debate.
Mr. Speaker, this is about all that I shall be able to say because we have this previous question hanging over our heads to muzzle us, but I think that, for us, parliamentarians, and also for yourself, Mr. Speaker, who are a distinguished parliamentarian and have been a Member for some time, it would have been interesting if those who have been sitting here for many years could have heard what the new Members, especially on the Government side, had to say about this bill, which they must consider essential since they want it to be passed immediately.
Investment Canada Act
This is therefore an important bill. As for us, and I do not think that the Members opposite have any reason to question our sincerity, we do not believe that agreeing to it would be in the interests of Canada which is an independent country with the right to protect itself, as do our friends from Great Britain, from France, but especially from the United States. Mr. Speaker, it is on this point that I shall conclude before leaving the floor to my colleague from Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), if you want to recognize him, or else I could invite my colleagues from the Government to rise.
Mr. Speaker, it is not in the interests of Canada that the Americans believe that, under this new Government led by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), whom we respect, the door is now wide open in Canada, that all controls have been lifted, that we beg them to come here, to create jobs, to reduce jobs, and to keep research and technology in their own country. We have evidence of this. In Canadian companies with less than 50 employees, 11 per cent of the research is done in Canada and 3 per cent abroad. In companies with 50 to 100 employees, 10 per cent of the research is done in Canada, but when these companies are foreign-controlled, the figure is 4 per cent. In companies with 500 employees, 10 per cent of the research is done in Canada, but 2 per cent is done in-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member, but the time allotted to him has expired. The Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien).

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to return to the House today. I see we are involved in a procedural wrangle in which the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) is using his young Parliamentary Secretary (Mrs. Tardif) to do his dirty work. Frankly, I can sympathize with the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg, because as the House may recall, I was once Minister of Finance in this House-

When I was Minister of Finance my critic was the Member who is Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) today. We had a debate in the House which lasted 15 weeks. He was still asking questions and complaining about when I would get up rather than asking my Parliamentary Secretary to get up and do a little job. I got up and said that that was enough, after 15 weeks we had to vote.
I was in the House all the time. We have not seen the Minister in the House. Where is he today? Is he closing factories in Quebec? Is he selling Canada out to the Americans? He prepared the speech that the Prime Minister will use to sing for the American bigshots in Baie Comeau. He went to New York to sing again a few weeks ago with a speech prepared by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. He is

January 30, 1985
Investment Canada Act
not in the House to do his job. Where is he today when the Government is imposing closure after 14 hours of debate? He is running away and asking a Member of Parliament to do his dirty job. Where are they on the other side?

Those Messrs. Muffler who when they were in the Opposition complained because we used closure once or twice after twenty weeks of debate . . . They are not complaining today. I will say this for the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne): He is not a Mr. Muffler. In fact, he said he was a "deux de pique", a two of spades, and I suppose his neighbour is the three of diamonds. Where are they, all those silent Conservative Members who were elected in Quebec? The Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif), who said herself that she was used by her Minister and was not familiar with the procedure. I found this so outrageous that I felt obliged to take the floor, Mr. Speaker.
And when you consider the policy of the Conservatives! Today we have seen once again the confusion about metric and non-metric. They said they were going to do away with FIRA and they created a new agency called Investment Canada. Americans may be obliged to file applications after all. They tell them they will not when they are in the United States, and then they table legislation in Parliament that will maintain the obligation to apply to a Government agency for permission to invest in Canada.
Of course we want foreign investment, but not at the cost of our national pride. It was humiliating for Canadians to see what happened in New York a few weeks ago, when the Prime Minister of Canada sang for his supper to entertain New York businessmen. But where is this investment today? Since the Progressive Conservatives came to power, in the Saint-Mau-rice area alone, which I represent, Melchers closed its doors in Berthier, Wabasso and Westinghouse closed down in Trois-Rivieres and Wabasso, Le Carbure and C.I.L. in Shawinigan. These industries are Shawinigan's lifeblood. And I could mention many similar occurrences in the region, like the one that caused the Member for Champlain-good for him-to say that this region had become a disaster area since the Progressive Conservatives came to power. We had several plans for the Saint-Maurice area, including the electrochemical research center for Shawinigan, which was cancelled, the agricultural research center for the riding of Trois-Rivieres, also cancelled, and the agricultural research center for Victoriaville, cancelled as well. And now what is happening? At least 2,000 jobs have been lost in central Quebec alone, since the Progressive Conservatives came to power. Where are last summer's demagogues who said we were doing nothing for Quebec? Where are the Members who were elected to bring investment to Quebec, and to create jobs for Quebecers? They are silent! They have been silenced, Mr. Speaker, as effectively as Mr. Muffler silences cars on TV.
The Minister is smiling, but we have not heard him say much about Quebec's economic problems. Not a word today,
and we are paying the price for their silence. The only policy they have is to get on their knees and ask the Americans to come and invest in this country. They will come if there are any profits to be made in Canada. They are not going to come because we get down on our knees. If we are proud to be Canadians, we cannot go to the Americans as we are doing today and say: Come and take what you want in Canada, it is free. They will not respect us for it. They will come if they can make money. They are not going to come because they like the way we smile. And meanwhile, what is happening to this country?
I have just come back from a trip to the far East, and people are wondering whether there still is a Canada or whether we have become an extension of the United States. I asked this question the other day, and it is becoming increasingly clear that the only thing the Prime Minister of Canada wants is to try to please the Americans and become the first Governor of the State of Canada.
In any case, let us talk about external affairs. Last week, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) apparently forgot that last fall the House indicated quite clearly that we were against the American star wars policy. At that time, the Opposition agreed with the Government and the House was unanimous on that truly important international policy. But since Reagan told Mulroney: We want you on our side, everything changed and our contribution simply vanished. The various parties in the House of Commons had managed to reach a consensus concerning our position on the international peace policy, but the Americans in New York spoke to Mulroney and once again the issue is settled. Here we are today, after hardly fourteen hours of debate, Mr. Speaker, you have been in this House long enough-

Mr. Speaker, I see that the Conservatives are touchy. I must say that it is shameful, because we are taking decisions about the future of Canada and I am really asking myself just what kind of economic policy we will have in this country. Who will decide for Canada when it comes to jobs, research and development? What is going on in the House? The scandalous aspect of all this is that the Minister has gone into hiding after
January 30, 1985

asking his Parliamentary Secretary to put the previous question. This is unprecedented in the House, the Ministers do not take their responsibilities. It is unheard of, they impose closure after only fourteen hours of debate on an extremely important measure which has not been the subject of consultation throughout Canada. They have been saying all along:

"We will consult with everybody". I don't know who was consulted about the Bill. Not even Members of Parliament were consulted. The Conservatives consulted the business community in New York probably but not Canadian businessmen.
What effect will this Bill have on some parts of Canada? In the northern United States people are complaining because jobs are going from Michigan or New Hampshire down to the sun belt. What will happen to us when we are even farther north if there is no border and no capacity to make decisions to protect our own jobs in Canada? What has been the result of six months of free enterprise mentality? It has been an absolute disaster in the Province of Quebec. In the last three months one factory after another has been closing.
The Minister will not discuss options with anyone and will not intervene to save jobs. He will just let the Americans take over all of Canada. I believe that there is still a place in this land for this Parliament to express views about what the economic policy of this country should be instead of the businessmen of New York, deciding that.

Mr. Speaker, initially 1 would like to welcome the Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) back to the House from the corporate boardrooms of Toronto. It is a pleasure to see him putting in a guest appearance in the House and we certainly welcome him back after that kind of performance.
I am delighted to take part in the debate on this fundamental question. Again, it is with some interest that I have been listening to Liberal Members of Parliament, including the Member for Saint-Maurice, speak on this question. I recall very vividly when we on this side of the House in opposition, along with our Tory colleagues in opposition, rose time and again to question the Government about shutdowns of corporations right across this land. It was that Liberal Minister and that Liberal Government that said it was the market that was taking the role and they were responding to market forces. That kind of hypocrisy surely is not acceptable to the people of Canada.
The Liberals talk with ringing indignation about the fact that Canada must not take its orders from the boardrooms of New York, Hartford and elsewhere in the United States. If one looks at the foreign policy of that former Government and the decision with respect to the testing of the Cruise missile, for example, where are those great defenders of the autonomy of Canada today? Just a few months ago they were the ones who were defending the American economic policy, foreign policy and every other policy as well.
I remember questioning the former Minister of Regional Economic Expansion with respect to a company in my constit-
Investment Canada Act
uency that had shut down. It was one of the 98 per cent or 99 per cent of successful applications approved under the Foreign Investment Review Act of the previous Government. I had asked the Minister about the undertakings given by that company when it had received approval to take over this Canadian company. I was told that unfortunately those undertakings were not a matter of public record but were between the Government of Canada, FIRA, and the company. Even the 250 workers at that plant who lost their jobs were told that they had no right whatsoever to know the terms and conditions of that takeover.
Today, there is a Government which has come forward to say that it is effectively putting up the for sale sign. Canada is for sale to the highest bidder. If one examines the rather toothless wonder of FIRA and the very minimal conditions which were in effect, how can the Government possibly come before Parliament and suggest that it wants to destroy even the basic scrutiny that existed under the previous Government, inadequate though that may have been?
What were some of the questions which were asked of companies which sought to invest in Canada? The first question was whether this new investment would provide jobs for Canadians. I would have assumed that a foreign company coming to Canada would have been asked that as a basic question. Yet the Government, through this Bill, is saying that it does not care. If a company wants to come in and take over Canadian companies, the Government puts down the welcome mat. If the company decides to shut down that plant six months later because of its world product mandate, its desire to maximize profits globally and to open up where there is cheaper labour, no environmental or labour standards or no unions, the Government says that that is fair enough because that is free enterprise in action.
It is free enterprise in action but if we look at the record of foreign capital in this country, it has been a record that has resulted in the net loss of thousands of jobs. It has been one which has resulted in research and development in Canada being at one of the lowest levels of any industrialized country in the western world.
Of course, if there are foreign corporations in Canada they will not do R and D in Canada; they will conduct their research and development at their head office in the United States. Historically, Mr. Speaker, foreign companies have viewed Canada as a cheap source of raw materials and as a lucrative market for their goods and services.
The fundamental decisions which have been taken about investment, about employment, about research and development, about export, new technology and marketing, have not been taken here in Canada by Canadians in the interests of Canadians; they have been taken in foreign boardrooms not in the interests of Canadians but in the interest of the global profit picture, the bottom line, of a multinational corporation.
What this Conservative Government is doing in paying off its friends in the corporate boardroom is saying let's have more

January 30, 1985
Investment Canada Act
of the same. Let's sell out Canada. Let's sell out Canada even more than we have already sold it out. We in this Party say that is fundamentally unacceptable.
I see a Tory back-bencher who wants to speak, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest that he might want to take the opportunity while this debate lasts to rise to his feet and defend the policies of this Government which is effectively throwing open the doors to foreign capital and ending any meaningful control by Canadians over investment in Canada. I suspect we will not hear very much from the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) aside from the bleating coming from the backbenchers. The word has gone out. This Government has been secretive, yet it purports to reflect the views expressed on parliamentary reform and a new era in Parliament. But what have the Tories done on one of the most important Bills to face the people of Canada? They have shut down debate. That is a shameful action and the people of Canada will remember the silence of Tory back-benchers when it comes to the next election.
There is no question that this debate is an historic debate because it touches upon the future and who will be making decisions about Canadian resources and Canadian jobs. We do not need more studies to show the level of destruction to our economy as a result of the fact that basically we are tenants in our own land. There has been lots of documentation about that. There was the Gordon Commission in the 1950s, the Watkins report in the 1960s, and the Gray report in the 1970s, all of which documented very clearly the problems that foreign investment creates in this country.
The question then must be asked, who is going to control the economic decision-making in this country? The answer which appears to be given by the Tories is-
Wall Street.

-that we do not care any more because ultimately wherever the bottom line reigns that will be where the Tory Party is prepared to accept foreign investment.
The Liberal approach to foreign ownership was not significantly better, but at least the Liberals did not propose to dismantle FIR A. Ed Lumley, a former Minister, said that Canada was one of the most open countries in the world. I cannot imagine another country that is more generous in its treatment of foreign investors. We in this House have seen hundreds of thousands of Canadians losing jobs as a result of throwing Canada open to foreign ownership by this Government and the previous Government. We have seen the contradiction in policy. On the one hand the Government talks about reducing the deficit, but in the next breath it brings in this Bill which will increase the deficit because it will result in a net outflow of dividends and interest payments. It is time that we in this country took control of our own economy for Canadians and by Canadians.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be appropriate to identify what this debate is all about and remember that it is Standing Order 56(1) that is being referred to right now, and that it requires that the previous question be put.
As Hon. Members will remember, that motion was put by the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister. We regret that once more the Minister does not have the guts, the courage to do his own work in this House. We have very seldom seen him here since the debate started. And looking back at the Members who participated, I think the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) was right when he called the Government Members "mufflers", because they have not been very articulate in this debate that is most important to us.
Looking at Hansard, Mr. Speaker-and I would like to say this for the record-there were only a few hours of debate, three hours and 12 minutes to be more accurate, used by the Progressive Conservatives, as against 10 hours and 51 minutes for the Liberals, and 9 hours and 19 minutes for the New Democratic Party. I would not say that 22 hours of debate is
January 30, 1985

something excessive for such an important piece of legislation, and certainly not a reason for the Government to impose closure. The Government has 211 Members, who say nothing because they have nothing to say. That conclusion is obvious because they have not spoken. But we have much to say on the Bill, and we insist that our democratic rights be respected in this House. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, we will oppose and vote against Government closure.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to being a muzzle, the Standing Order prevents any person, any Member from introducing amendments to the legislation. This second reading stage, is traditionally the stage for consideration of the principle of the legislation, that is when the House may discuss the principle of the Bill.
I had expected the Government to be interested in hearing the views of all Members, but as I said, such is not the case. Indeed, I am very much amazed that the Hon. Members from Ottawa-Carleton, my area, have not risen in this debate, except for one. And I thought the Hon. Members for Ottawa-West and Nepean-Carleton would speak up because in their constituencies, in the Ottawa area, there is a major high technology industry, an industry that has created many jobs.
Mr. Speaker, it will be remembered that the Hon. Member for York-Peel, when he introduced the Bill, said that the impact of Bill C-15 would be to create jobs.
But looking at the media, or at the comments made at the time by the Hon. Members, we realize it is not quite accurate to claim that this change or name substitution will mean any great contribution to job creation. I am thinking, among other things, about a report in the December 20, 1984, issue of The Globe and Mail in which it was suggested that the big American financiers would not be in any great hurry to come and invest here, and 1 would simply like to quote from that report in English:

-foreign investors are a hard-nosed lot interested in making money. In Canada, that means mainly resource industries, and, with the exception of oil and gas, resources are not considered good investments.
The world is producing too much of raw materials, such as copper, nickel, and certain kinds of lumber, which Canada traditionally has produced.

Concerning funds those Americans supposedly would invest in Canada, I am quoting once more from Mr. Thomas Wal-kom in The Globe and Mail:
"You don't get the idea that there are a lot of folks with money bags at the border, waiting to get into Canada", said a banker, smiling wryly.
"People in Canada are going to have to be very patient," ... "Investment will be up, but not necessarily enough to do anything about unemployment."

I did not say that: an American banker, one of the Prime Minister's friends in New York did. Thus, we must not rely
Investment Canada Act
upon the United States to bring us money or jobs. I read also in the House of Commons Hansard a comment on clause 21 made by my friend from Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Barry Turner), in which he says about jobs and investments:
Capital resources in Canada are not sufficient to meet the needs of governments, whether federal, provincial or municipal, nor those of the private sector.
Therefore, we have on the one hand a statement saying we need money and on the other, American bankers who say: We have money but we may not be in as much of a hurry as you think.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) said when he rose in this House:

I would just like to point out that for three months our Party has been talking positively about an opportunity ... for foreigners to invest in this country ... unemployment has gone down. There were 100.000 new jobs started up.
To him I must say that one cannot be so naive as to think that sweet-talk can create 100,000 jobs. We all know that there is a six-month lag in economics and that jobs come after a certain time. The result, the jobs about which he bragged, were indeed created by policies of the former Liberal Government in months gone by. As a matter of fact, if we look at the statistics we Find that the number of jobs created in the last few months is no greater than the jobs created in previous months.
A more interesting statement was made by a friend of the Tories, Mr. James Gillies, a former Member of this House. I refer to an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail in which Mr. Gillies talked about capital flow and job creation. 1 think this article is worth reading. It is enlightening in terms of foreign investment. In part it read:
Not all foreign investment is productive. It is naive to believe that any flow of capital into the country will move the economy forward. It depends entirely on what it is used for. If it is not invested in the production of new plant and equipment and does not lead to an increase in exports it can have serious negative economic consequences.
I am not the one who said that. It was Mr. James Gillies, an expert economist and a former Tory Member of the House. He continued:
Moreover, until the intractable balance of payments problem is solved we must try to limit the borrowing of capital from abroad. No government or government agency should borrow in foreign markets under current conditions. If a government has a function that it believes must be performed either directly or through a government agency, the capital should be raised domestically or the proposed operation should be postponed.
I thought that statement was rather interesting. It was published in a January, 1985 edition of The Globe and Mail.
The auctioneer of some of our assets in Canada-I am thinking about Canadair, de Havilland, Teleglobe and other companies of that nature-Mr. Paul Marshall, was given the job of trying to sell, if he could, these companies to prospective buyers. We were told by the media in a recent report in The Citizen that Mr. Paul Marshall, President of the Canada Development Corporation, made a statement to the effect that

January 30, 1985
Investment Canada Act
there were no job guarantees in these possible sales. As a matter of fact, to quote Mr. Marshall, he said: "There are no job guarantees at this point". One would wonder why the Government would want to get rid of some of our good Crown assets without some guarantee of job security for those employed by these companies. The Government has been giving us promises of jobs, but evidently it has not been carrying out its promises. At this time it is not preaching by example when it puts on the block companies which are Canadian and which are Canadian assets, in my view.
I will just end my remarks by saying that we oppose this motion and regret it immensely.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to talk about this Bill. I think it is a very poor and misguided one. I want to put my concerns on record on behalf of my constituents.
It has been said that Canadians do not care whether a company is foreign owned or Canadian owned so long as it gives them jobs. Rather, I think it is because Canadians care very much about jobs that they have to look at the issue whether the company is foreign owned or domestically owned. Foreign-owned corporations do not provide as much employment and indeed are responsible for many unemployment problems in the country. As a result of control by foreign head offices, decisions are made that result in jobs disappearing, research and development jobs not being created here, and spin-off jobs which come from the purchase of other Canadian goods and services not going to Canadians because of the number of imports.
The situation with which we were faced before Bill C-15, before this dismantling of FIRA, was not an adequate one. We do not have a strong FIRA. It is something of a token operation. We would like to see FIRA strengthened. It was not adequate as it was set up. Of course it has been declining in its operations. It has been almost rubber-stamping applications, not looking after the interest of Canadians in finding jobs.
Our response to the inadequacies of FIRA would not be in the direction of this Bill. It would be in precisely the opposite direction. FIRA has not been strong enough. It has not been doing enough. There have not been the other measures which the Government should be introducing to buck up FIRA and to provide a context within which Canadians could begin to regain control of their economy.
Recently I returned from visiting Atlantic Canada and Regina with the NDP caucus action group on jobs. We met with a very large number of community groups. They spoke to us about their concerns about high unemployment in the country. I did not hear one group, individual, expert or specialist ask us to get rid of FIRA, to dismantle it or to weaken it. However, I heard from many individuals, experts, economists, political scientists, people running co-ops, small-business people, people active in the economic life of their communities and unemployed people who want to be active in the economic life of their communities. They talked about greater control of the Canadian economy. They talked about co-ops and small
businesses. They talked about job creation at home and manufacturing concerns which would buy goods and services in their communities and keep money in their communities. They talked about foreign corporations coming into their communities, making a bundle largely on the extraction of resources and then leaving. Of course, this is what foreign corporations can do. They talked about profits not being plowed back into their communities as a result of foreign ownership.
I heard quite an earful about the difficulties we already have with foreign investment and foreign control of our economy. People want less of it, not more. They want local control. They want the money to stay in their communities. They want jobs there. They want all the surrounding goods and services and the diversification which comes when companies operating in their communities are Canadian controlled, buy from their neighbours in the community and help keep the economy going.
We have a number of very fundamental problems. We have to look at the differences between foreign-controlled and Canadian-controlled corporations and at why foreign-controlled ones are not beneficial to our economy. First I point out that foreign-controlled firms import much more than Canadian-controlled ones. This reduces purchases in communities, jobs which go along with those purchases and spin-off benefits accruing from doing business within communities. This occurs particularly with the purchase of machinery and other high-level kinds of purchases.
Foreign companies imported 22 per cent of their sales, five times that of Canadian-controlled companies. In manufacturing, foreign-controlled companies imported 30 per cent of their sales, four times more than Canadian companies. Why do we want more of our economy controlled by corporations that will import more? It will simply mean job loss.
The second problem that arises with the differences between foreign-controlled and Canadian-controlled corporations concerns the disproportionate share of payments for non-merchandise items like interest payments, profits and service and management charges. The resources available for potential investment and job creation here in Canada are reduced by the outflow of interest payments, dividends, profits and so forth to head offices. This affects Canada's balance of payments and means that there will be less money available. The money is going out of the country to pay for management services which could well be provided by Canadians. That means that less money is left in the Canadian economy to be reinvested in an attempt to create more jobs.
Specifically, American-controlled firms holding 36 per cent of industrial assets in Canada accounted for 61 per cent of the external remittances. These remittances are going from foreign-controlled corporations and specifically American ones right across the border to the head offices. The Canadian corporations, to a much greater extent, are finding the management services and other services they need in Canada and they are paying out their interest payments, their profits and
January 30, 1985

their dividends to other Canadians who will be reinvesting that money in the country.
The third structural problem that exists with foreign-con-trolled corporations is that they do not spend nearly as much as Canadian-controlled corporations on research and development. This reveals a great deal of hypocrisy on the part of the Government which has indicated that it wants more research and development. This is true of the previous Government as well. We certainly apprised that Government of the problem and it said that it was concerned about research and development. Of course, it did very little about it.
Any increase in foreign control of the economy will mean that less research and development will be taking place in Canada, and of course that means there will be fewer job opportunities for Canadians who are involved in research and development. There are many people with Ph.D.s in all kinds of specialties who are unemployed. People who are well trained in research fields are driving taxis or doing part-time jobs and not using the talents they developed because they cannot get jobs. Where are those jobs? The jobs are attached to head offices in another country. Canadians do not receive these very important jobs. Indeed, the investment we have made in educating these people and developing their skills is lost to the Canadian economy.
An analysis of research and development expenditures of different sized corporations has been done and it indicates that the very large corporations, the ones we would expect to be contributing the most to research and development, are actually contributing the least. The relationship of research and development over sales for Canadian corporations with more than 500 employees is 10.3 per cent. That same ratio for foreign-owned corporations is 2 per cent. In other words, there is roughly a five-fold difference. These are the companies to which we look particularly for doing research and development in Canada.
The next problem I would like to raise is that the high rate of foreign control of Canadian industry contributes to poor productivity performance by reducing competition. Foreign subsidiaries do not face competition from their parent firms. This is a fact of life in the branch plant system. Branch plants operating in Canada are not meant to compete with parent companies but are meant to purchase, often at inflated prices, the products of the parent company and other affiliates in the system. They are not meant to put other products for which they have done research and development which would compete with the parent corporation on the market because it is the profits of the parent corporation which count in the economic decision-making process, not the profits of the branch plant. A branch plant that could be innovative and could compete is not allowed to do so because that is not a part of the branch plant system.
Specifically, foreign-controlled companies account for 72 per cent of all merchandise imports to Canada. That is what foreign-controlled companies are supposed to do. They are supposed to be importing rather than exporting and competing. A great deal of economic analysis has been done about
Investment Canada Act
this by government departments, Statistics Canada, and of course by a large number of independent researchers who have made very, very clear this very important structural problem.
The last of the problems of a structural nature that I wish to raise is that the greater dependence of foreign-controlled firms on merchandise imports which are usually tied to the parent company at the exclusion of Canadian competitors has the effect of reducing jobs available to Canadians. Studies done by the United States Senate and the Harvard Business School have found that direct American investment in Canada produces a significant net creation of jobs for all sectors of the United States workforce. That is lovely for the United States workforce but what is this Parliament doing maximizing job opportunities for American workers at the expense of Canadian workers?
We must be concerned about the high unemployment rate in our own country. To be in favour of a measure that will increase unemployment for our own people is simply scandalous at this time of high unemployment. It means that workers of all kinds, from research and development specialists to blue collar workers, will lose job opportunities because of the structure of the branch plant system. It extracts resources from Canada. Branch plants do the hewing of wood and drawing of water in Canada and keep the manufacturing and research and development at head office.
Even as it exists today, FIRA has certainly not been a tough check on foreign investment in Canada. FIRA approval rates over the past two years have been in the order of 95 per cent to 98 per cent. It is not as if we can say that the current FIRA has been screening out a great deal of foreign investment. Less than half of those foreign takeover applications that were approved were intended to increase investment or provide any new jobs, and that is a very crucial point.
Corporations that received approval under the existing FIRA did not provide opportunities for job creation. They did not represent new investment or expansion and they certainly did not represent greater productivity and the possibility of exports, innovations, or anything of that sort. They were simply takeovers. In some cases these takeovers even reduced production in Canada. We know that that happens. A company takes over a Canadian plant and a year later, in spite of everything that has been said to FIRA by the corporation, closes down the plant and jobs are lost. There are plenty of instances of foreign corporations entering Canada without even pretending that they will help the Canadian economy.
The current FIRA has not been careful enough in seeing that foreign investment on balance does good things for the Canadian economy. It has not even acted according to its own current terms of reference. In the future we can expect Investment Canada to do an even worse job unless there are major amendments to this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-15 is the first major piece of government legislation that has been

Investment Canada Act
put before us. It provides Canadians very quickly with knowledge of the philosophical bent that handcuffs the Conservative Party.
The debate over FIRA versus Investment Canada is a classic example of something which distinguishes a Liberal Government from a Conservative Government. First, FIRA was an instrument of nation building. It was an instrument to safeguard and promote Canadians and Canadian economic sovereignty. Investment Canada will do neither.
Second, while foreign investment was viewed as an indispensable sector of the economic pie, FIRA was an initiative taken by Canadians to put Canadians first. It was an initiative that attempted to instil in Canada a sense of purpose, vitality and leadership. Investment Canada will merely perpetuate the often heard criticism that Canada lacks the drive and self-fortitude to make things happen.
Third, FIRA put Canada second to no one. It viewed Canada and the United States as co-tenants of the North American continent. Investment Canada views the United States as the owner and Canada as the subservient tenant.
In short, FIRA subscribed to the theory that the ability to control the economy makes a strong economy, and also defines the kind of country we are and indeed want to be. Through Investment Canada we will lose that sense of national will and purpose. The economic subservience theory which is espoused by the new Government will not ensure long-term economic growth; it will merely transfer it to other lands and other peoples. It will only help boost the value of the American buck, the Eurodollar and the Japanese yen. Canadians are asking: "What about us?"
In reality Bill C-15 is yet another example of government which is far more interested in the art of public relations than it is in actual substance. This Government is prepared to sacrifice long-term economic planning and economic sovereignty for short-term, image-making propaganda. The Minister who introduced the legislation late last year declared in his press statement:
We are back in business. This legislation sends a message to the world that, once again, Canada welcomes investment.
Of what world does this Minister speak? This country has always been open for business and has always welcomed investment. If that were not the case, we would not be witnesses to what is a great, prosperous and thriving nation. In terms of economic investment, like any other country, under a Liberal Government, and specifically through FIRA, Canada wanted and stressed what was good for Canada and Canadians. Is that a negative attitude to take as a country? Is that not how a country attains a degree of respect in the international business community?
FIRA was an essential and calculated policy instrument which sought to ensure that foreign investment also included significant benefits to Canada. FIRA allowed Canadians to bargain and negotiate with a huge variety of multinational interests from a point of strength. The objective of FIRA was
January 30, 1985
not to prevent or discourage foreign investment, but rather to cater to it and to the needs and aspirations of Canada.
It should be noted that since its inception in 1974 FIRA has approved, on average, 92 per cent of all applications. That figure clearly demonstrates that foreign investors not only wanted to and did invest heavily in Canada, but that they were willing to meet the criteria which were established by FIRA. In short, the investors realized and appreciated that more jobs for Canadians, more research and development for Canada and greater Canadian exports were parts of the investment deal. Why should it be any different today?
It is doubtful that FIRA discouraged in a significant way any foreign investor who was serious about investing his or her capital in Canada. In fact, the Conference Board of Canada performed a study last April which determined that FIRA provided a deterrent for only 11 per cent of foreign business. More important, Statistics Canada figures indicate that FIRA did not halt the flow of U.S. investment into Canada. In fact, the gross inflow of direct U.S. investment into Canada continued to expand during the time of FIRA. Gross inflows varied between $1 billion and $1.4 billion throughout most of the 1970s, before sky-rocketing during 1980 and 1981. If we took a quick analysis of the facts and figures, we would find that they effectively contradict the Government's blind portrayal that FIRA was the enemy of foreign investment and that the removal of FIRA, replaced by Investment Canada, would bring a new beginning.
As the Bill stands, direct acquisitions by non-Canadians of businesses in Canada with assets of less than $5 million are not subject to review; neither are indirect takeovers resulting from the acquisition of parent companies outside Canada when the Canadian subsidiary has assets of over $50 million. In my opinion, that is a grave concern for Canadian small businessmen, particularly in the increasingly competitive field of high technology. The Government will simply open the doors and allow the takeover of firms which are below these thresholds. What will Canada gain if these small enterprises are more prone to shutdowns? What will we gain if these Canadian jobs are not guaranteed? What steps will be available to the Canadian Government to prevent such economic hardships? What action can the Government take to guarantee benefits to Canada and to ensure jobs for all Canadians? Unfortunately the answer to those questions is that this Government wishes to wash its hands of its commitment to small businessmen.
Another case which illustrated FIRA's protection for small businessmen involved the terms which were negotiated when the Herald Company of Syracuse, New York, a publishing Firm, took over Random House of Canada Limited. As a result of FIRA, the American buyer agreed to guarantee the jobs of all 85 Random House employees and to offer jobs to ten employees of another Canadian company which was closing its Mississauga plant. In addition, the Canadian employees of Random House were to be given a chance to buy a controlling interest in the company. Finally, the buyer agreed to print in Canada any book it published when Canadian sales were expected to exceed 10,000 copies. Those economic concessions
January 30, 1985

will no longer be possible with Investment Canada. Many firms which are below the new thresholds may be small, but collectively they are the engine and the spirit behind the creation of new jobs in Canada.
To further compound the inequities of Investment Canada, the larger takeovers which will dictate the fate of thousands of workers and the interests of entire regions will now rest at the mercy of one Minister. Under FIRA those factors would be shared by the full Cabinet in order to incorporate and understand a variety of disciplines, interests and regional necessities. That perspective was much more encompassing. Now, a billion dollar decision in the hands of one Minister centralizes power in an unprecedented way. In doing so, it imposes horrendous limitations as it relates to the spectrum of interests.
Not only is the concept that FIRA discouraged foreign investment a fabricated myth perpetuated by the Tories, but that inaccuracy is also complemented by a mood that at the present time the U.S. is least likely to undergo active investment abroad. This growing view was echoed in a fascinating article in The Globe and Mail. I realize, Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time has ended. Perhaps, if this debate is extended, I could read that fascinating article to the House at another time.

Mr. Speaker, this is a day which should be marked and underlined with a red pencil in the annals of the new Mulroney Government. We are seeing the gagging of Parliament. We are seeing another form of retreat from those brave, bold words of July, which turned into shambles and tatters by the time we reached January. They are the great paragons of parliamentary rights.
Without a doubt, this is one of the most critical pieces of legislation which has been brought forward in many a year. After a limited debate of not more than 20 hours, this grand majority-those 211 Members-are putting their tails between their legs and retreating into the last refuge of scoundrels-the right to close off debate. Why? Because they are afraid of what they are hearing. Government Members do not like what is being said in this Parliament about the inadequacies and fallabilities of the Government's approach to the Investment Canada Bill.
We on this side are not surprised at that. The Government started out with a broken promise. I would like to quote from an interesting article from The Calgary Herald, which of course I read faithfully every day. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), who was then the Opposition critic, was asked what the Conservatives would do about the Foreign Investment Review Agency if elected. He said that he would not like to say what the changes would be but that there would be public hearings. He continued:
Those public hearings will be held before a Tory government drafts new legislation-
Well, we were all waiting for the public hearings, but in the darkness of night the Minister sailed into the House, laid the legislation on the Table and we have not seen him since. The House has heard all this debate, but where has the Minister
Investment Canada Act
been? This Government that wants to consult and hear from people has discriminated against Members of Parliament. It does not want to hear from its own Members of Parliament or from us. The Minister has not bothered to show up, nor has the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). This Bill is the centre piece, the crown jewel of its economic program, and Ministers of the Government cannot be bothered to take a minute or two away from working with their chiefs of staff to come here and listen to the debate. Instead, they are going to close off the debate.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, they are closing it off because they realize and recognize that it is a faulty and flawed piece of legislation which does not do the job it is supposed to do. It has nothing to do with investment in Canada. It has to do with some punitive, vindictive response to what Government thought were the inadequacies of the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
The debate thus far has shown some very serious flaws in the Bill which the Canadian people are now beginning to recognize. When has there ever been a piece of legislation which has given such uncontrolled power to make discretionary decisions on major plant locations and economic development to one Minister without any recourse to Cabinet, to Parliament or to any committee? He has been set up as an economic czar and he does not have to answer to anyone. That is incredible power, and if I were a member of the Conservative Party I would be a little concerned because those Hon. Members will also suffer the same limitation of access as any other Canadian. We know how inaccessible the Minister is. He is never in the House, so I do not know when his colleagues see him. I can tell you one thing, Mr. Speaker, to provide one Minister with that kind of power is asking for trouble, and those Hon. Members opposite are going to find it in spades. On what basis will decisions be made: on who paid his Tory membership last month, or on who was talked to at the latest dinner for the old alumni of the Bank of Western Canada? Who is going to get the benefit of that particular kind of examination? We do not know, Mr. Speaker, and neither will any other Canadian.
We know very clearly, Mr. Speaker, that in this Bill there is power to make decisions which will affect regions. Nothing is more critical to economic development, and yet here we have a Minister who has shown time and time again his insensitivity to regional development. He does not understand the word. He can only see so far from when he sits on his horse farm somewhere north of Toronto. He has nothing to do with what is going on in Atlantic Canada because we see there the evisceration of all the regional development investments which made sense.
What is the reason for all this, Mr. Speaker? We know the price we will have to pay and we are still taking cap in hand, doffing it to our American friends and saying, "We are wide open for business". It is a doormat policy which we are encountering day after day in this House. We see it in every respect. We saw the Minister of National Defence (Mr. January 30, 1985

Investment Canada Act
Coates) selling out on the DEW line question, initialling agreements open to totally unintended consequences. We saw the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), that one-time red Tory, who is now turning an indescribable purplish shade, rising in his place to say, "Oh, I agree with star wars. That is one of the great advances towards world peace". So we are going to have a star wars philosophy because that is going to help and encourage negotiations. To spend $40 billion or $50 billion on a brand new weapons system in outer space somehow, in the logic of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is going to help maintain world peace. I have more respect for that Minister than that. I suspect he has simply been given his orders by the Prime Minister not to disrupt those kind and cordial relations with the President of the United States, which the Prime Minister says he wants to establish in order to make sure we get a better economic deal.
But, Mr. Speaker, what have been the results of that sort of cap in hand, doormat approach which Government has taken? We just heard today in Question Period in the House of Commons that in return for our investment, in return for our so-called open hand, the Americans are going to increase substantially the tariffs on cod fish, which will only affect the entire economy of eastern Canada. In particular, the constituency of the Prime Minister is going to be one of those areas which will be affected in the most dire and drastic way. But it is all right that our American friends are going to increase the tariff by 25 per cent.
Last week we heard of the decision of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) to take off the export surcharge on gasoline or heavy oil to the United States. What will Canadians pay? They are going to pay $6 a barrel more. I believe this Government, Mr. Speaker, is headed toward a very thorny patch. What disturbs us, of course, is that it does not know what the consequences are. What we are seeing is a haphazard, ad hoc, confused approach to government. Those Ministers are making decisions when they get up on their feet, if then. They are contradicting one another and do not have any kind of clearly enunciated strategy about how we can develop the economy of this country. The Americans themselves, the Conference Board of Canada and the American Wall Street brokers, have all said that this legislation will not add one additional cent to the foreign investment coming into Canada. They say there are other kinds of problems. Last year under the old FIRA program $4.3 billion came into Canada. And there was, however, a difference, Mr. Speaker, we had the ability and capacity under that program to ensure that there would be benefits and jobs for Canadians, that there would be research and development in Canada, and that there would be good management. But this Government is giving up that right. It is giving up the power to bargain for a better deal for Canadians. Its so-called open window, open sesame approach is simply a way of saying-

I think there is some kind of Irish conspiracy going on and we will have to trace it back to some sort of
Fenian plot in the 19th century in order to explain the Mulroney-Reagan love-in affair, the amorous union that is taking place daily, which results in absolutely no form of protection for Canadians. That is the problem with which we are faced. We are getting into these new liaisons which result for Canadians in the loss of their birthright. We are losing our birthright. No economic development is going to take place. There is nothing in the Bill to encourage Canadian investors. There is nothing to provide for protection for our small businesses. We have nothing to bargain with. Now Parliament is being snuffed out, debate is gagged, and we are told there is no point in even looking at the issues anymore.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we happen to believe that there are still a lot of very important issues. I can say on behalf of my caucus that if we are not allowed the privileges and rights as parliamentarians to debate this Bill any longer in this Chamber, we will certainly make full, proper and effective use of that right when we get to committee.
