Mr. Speaker, 1 find it somewhat amusing to sit and listen to Liberals making the same speeches about closure as I heard from Conservatives last year, the year before that and the year before that. If we have ever had evidence that there is really no difference between the Grits and Tories, we have had it today, and neither of the Parties had the courtesy to blush. I wish they would at least send their speeches back and forth across the way, then they could take turns making them every time we have closure in this House.
The issue is not whether we should have foreign investment. There is no argument that we need some foreign investment. What we need is more loan capital and less ownership or equity capital. I like the American people, all of us do. They are good neighbours and good friends. I like my own friends and relatives also, but I do not want them moving into my house so that I have to live in the garage. That is a quote from Tommy Douglas at the time we forced a minority Liberal Government to bring in foreign investment review. We ended up with a toothless tiger, but at least it was a beginning.
Canada is not alone in how it is treated by foreign investment. I had an opportunity to be in Mexico City and when I left I bought the Mexico City Daily News. On the financial page it says: "Foreign Firms Reaping Profits". Here is what happened in Mexico. Transnational companies operating in that country invested $273 million in the first six months of 1984. Those same companies sent out of Mexico $820 million in royalties, interest and profits during that same period, in other words, Mr. Speaker, almost quadruple their investment. And Mexico is a poor country. No one objects to foreign investors making a reasonable return, but any nation worthy of the name has to have some ground rules which put controls on the reinvestment of profits. These companies cannot just cut and run whenever they feel like it.
January 30, 1985

In that poor country of Mexico, in the two and a half years from the beginning of 1982 to the middle of 1984, United States corporate investment was $1.2 billion. In that same period of time, some $4.78 billion was sent back to the parent companies. That is nothing more than the bleeding of a poor nation. It is bad enough when they bleed a country like ours that is relatively well off, but they even do it to a poor country like Mexico.
I spoke about ground rules on foreign investment. Those ground rules must cover such things as how much profit is to be reinvested. They have to say that if you are a resource-based foreign-owned corporation with an operation in a one industry town, you shall pay a royalty into a fund to protect that town at a time when the resource has been depleted or the operation is not profitable. If the company wants to leave, there will be enough money there to ensure that the community will have funds available to be invested in some other industry and thus save the community from dying. That also needs to be applied to domestic corporations which think they can move into communities and pull out 20 years later, leaving them high and dry.
There need to be limits on how much the company can send back to the parent company by way of interest and dividend payments. There needs to be a requirement that a certain percentage of the total parent companies' spending on research and development must occur in the country in which they have branch plants. It cannot all be done in the home country. Without those kinds of ground rules, Mr. Speaker, we become nothing more than a territorial extension of the United States or of any other major foreign investor. Just as we have become a territorial extension of the United States militarily, we will also become a territorial extension economically. When you allow too much foreign ownership and control of your economy, you lose some of your economic sovereignty and national independence. It has happened before and it is bound to happen again if the Government insists on going ahead with this mindless pleading for foreign investment without there being sufficient ground rules.
There must be significant benefit to Canada Mr. Speaker. That is a key phrase. It was in place under FIRA. But the Government of those days did not make sure that it laid out the ground rules for FIRA to enforce. Unless and until we get those kinds of ground rules, we have to be more than once bitten and twice shy about foreign investment. We cannot just leave it to come and go for the sole benefit of an international corporation and to the detriment of our own nation.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that most Canadians are more concerned about our independence and sovereignty, our ability to exercise control, not only over our national policies as they relate to defence but over our economy as well. The minute we allow inordinate amounts of foreign ownership in one or more sectors of our economy, we have lost some of our sovereignty, our independence. No self-respecting parliamentarian can sit back and allow that to happen. We all believe in having good international relations. We are internationalists, but not at the
Investment Canada Act
expense of our own nationalism and our nationhood. We are not internationalists at the expense of our sovereignty.
You cannot blame the foreign investor or the foreign corporation for acting as it sees fit in the best interests of that corporation, when it is allowed to operate freely, or when there are no real ground rules for it to live up to. We cannot blame them; we have to blame ourselves. Successive free enterprise governments have, since before Confederation, gone on their hands and knees, begging and pleading foreign capital to control a major part of our economy. As a result, successive national Governments were immobilized in their ability to deal with booms, busts or anything in between as they ran the risk of incurring the anger of the Government of the nation where those foreign corporations were located. The United States has a long history, as did the British, French and German colonial powers, of exercising its power over countries like Canada at any time it thought its corporations and their investments in Canada might in any way be inhibited or reduced. The United States Government has always, as a matter of policy, be it Democratic or Republican, gone to bat for the major corporations which have controlled anywhere up to 90 per cent of any one sector of our economy.
I hope the Government will reconsider and present to the committee, if, as and when this Bill reaches it, a set of ground rules that we can all support. Then this so-called Investment Canada will be an even stronger agency than FIRA and it will be able to deal impartially with foreign investment for the benefit of our own country.

At that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that this country is open for business again. I had never felt that the country had ever been closed to business. I do not stand in the shadow of the Prime Minister in wanting to enhance and improve our trading relationship and friendhip with our great neighbour, the United States. On other occasions I have said to him that I do not envisage our relationship with the United States on the continent of North America to be one of proprietor and tenant, but, rather, one of two equal co-tenants sharing the resources, future and environment of the continent. Any enhancement of our relationship with our neighbour should not be made at the expense of an independent foreign policy for Canada, our political sovereignty, or our economic and cultural integrity. Those are the issues at stake in this particular Bill.
I said that I did not object to the Prime Minister saying that this country is open for business. However, I say once again, as I have said in the House and across the country, that Canada is not up for sale.
Hear, hear!

I am concerned, as are my colleagues, that the Government is not seriously considering its relationship with the United States in matters of defence. It is accepting, almost blindly, what the U.S. Secretary of Defence may say or the Pentagon may dictate. We have already spoken about the extension and destabilization of our weapons systems into star wars research.
Last week we in the House of Commons experienced the extraordinary phenomenon of my having to put a question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) following a committee session on Thursday during which the Conservative Members of the standing committee refused to allow the text of a treaty to be signed with the United States to be revealed to other Members of Parliament on that standing committee. I met the U.S. delegation which came to Ottawa on Monday to sign that treaty. I said that I was not in a position to make a comment because I had not had an opportunity to read the treaty. I said that at the appropriate time we would want to
know what concessions had been made to Alaskan fishermen that changed that treaty from the text which was defeated by the United States Senate two years ago.
I bring that to your attention as a relevant example, Mr. Speaker. This disregard for Parliament is without precedent. A treaty involving the fishermen on the West Coast was signed in Ottawa without any Member of Parliament or standing committee of the House of Commons having an opportunity to review it. I concede the argument of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that constitutionally the executive of Cabinet has the power to sign a treaty unless it has legislative consequences upon which Parliament or the provinces must act. However, a treaty is an important document. It has more validity and strength than a mere agreement, an exchange of notes or a contract. It binds two countries.
I have had some experience in negotiating treaties. I had the honour of being on the negotiating team for the Columbia River Treaty. The Hon. Paul Martin was the Secretary of State for External Affairs at that time and I was parliamentary secretary to the late Arthur Laing, whose riding of Vancouver South is now represented by the Minister of Fisheries. We took the position that the Columbia River Treaty need not be before Parliament for ratification as it had to go before the United States Senate under our constitutional precedents. Yet the treaty was of such importance that we sent it before the Standing Committee on External Affairs. The committee examined the treaty and heard witnesses on it for six weeks in order to convince the Canadian public that it was in the best interests of Canada.
This present treaty involved very sensitive issues. It involves the livelihood of the fisherpeople on the West Coast of the country as well as the sports fishermen. This treaty, involving a very important industry in British Columbia, has not even reached the floor of the House of Commons or a standing committee. That attitude is infectious in the Government. Moving that the previous question be put at this stage in the debate reflects the same disregard for the House of Commons.
This is the first major original piece of legislation brought to the House by the Government. It raises more questions than it answers with respect to foreign investment. It raises serious questions which need to be debated by the House. These questions have been brought to your attention and amply outlined by my colleagues. Are the levels of the review procedures too high? What is the impact on small Canadian independent business? What are the implications of the change in the benefit test from a "significant" benefit to Canada to a "net" benefit to Canada? These words may have a great consequence on the way in which this legislation will operate.
When we look at the assessment factors we see the same five factors as in the earlier legislation plus the inclusion of the words, "compatibility with cultural policy and effect on international competitiveness". What do those words mean? We have had insufficient review and explanation from the Government on that. Yet they are absolutely crucial to the operation

of this legislation because they are the factors upon which the agency bases its assessment.
What about the review process itself? What about the words "culturally sensitive factor"? The reserve power to review any investment, regardless of size, in culturally sensitive factors, is subject to that review process. What does "culturally sensitive" means? Once again there has been insufficient explanation given.
The issue of job creation was handled very eloquently by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. The Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) says that this legislation will bring investment flowing into the country, and thereby jobs. That is merely an assumption which has not been proven. As my colleague said, when the New York investment banking community was asked by members of the media from this country whether that would be the fact, they said no. This Bill will not change market factors or the unused industrial capacity in this country which militates against the investment we like to see. This piece of legislation will not change the debt-equity ratio of some of our major concerns for our smaller businesses, several hundreds of thousands of which were ravaged by the recession in this country. There is nothing in this Bill to encourage Canadian investment, yet the title of the Bill is "Investment Canada". That point was made very succinctly by my colleague from Laval-des-Rapides.

Member representing his or her many constituents. But the Minister responsible is not here. Ministers of the Crown are not there, except for a lone one.

He has been here for a long time. He is having problems in his riding with hog producers, but that is a different story. Only one minister . . . but not the Minister responsible, not the Prime Minister.
Decisions in this area used to be taken by the Cabinet as a whole. I am aware of the Minister's approach concerning our Crown corporations. He favours the clearance sale approach. He has not even determined under what terms Canadair, de Havilland, Eldorado Nuclear and Teleglobe Canada would be sold. Who would be the eligible buyers? At what price? What protection would there be for Canadian technology and, more importantly for Canadian workers, men and women? He does not say. Are we going to let that same minister control all by himself all foreign investment coming into Canada? What a risk. Well, the House would not have the time to hold a debate. Why is there not at least a committee of ministers? Why has the Minister of Finance no input in this regard?
Contrary to what the Minister had promised, there was no public consultation. We hear constantly in the House about this new government of consultation. It is eternal consultation to try and reach a consensus, but consultation without leadership. But in this area, there is no consultation. With the Americans maybe, but certainly not with Hon. Members of this House.

There has been no public consultation. The Government seems to be more concerned about pleasing the bankers on Wall Street, New York than the baker on Main Street, Canada.
I come now to the motion. Why is the Government so afraid of the Opposition that it has had to impose this heavy-handed measure to end the debate? The back-bench Conservative Members were elected from all parts of Canada with a huge majority and a massive mandate from the people of Canada. Why do we not hear from them? All that we hear is the flipping of the fins. Whenever the House Leader gives them the word, there is a standing ovation and applause for the Prime Minister.
There have been only 23 hours of debate on an issue of vital importance to Canadians. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) was here, but he has left the Chamber.
He is right there.
We are working.

The Minister and the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) who just spoke will recall that there were over 400 hours of debate on the Crow legislation. There were 400 hours of debate on that legislation, but only hours of debate on this legislation which is of very great significance to this country. Of those 23 hours, according to the rules, there were 11 hours used by Liberal speakers prior to this afternoon, 9.2 hours taken up by the New Democratic Party, and 3.2 hours used by the Conservative Party. Where is the respect for Parliament?
The Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has the responsibility for the committee on the reform of Parliament. No one on this side doubts his sincerity. We can recall the Conservative Members, when in opposition, calling for an enhanced role of the Member of Parliament. I believe in that enhanced role because each one of us is elected individually by people in this country, in ridings composed of 80,000, 100,000 or 120,000 people. I respect every Member in this House and while I do not think there is a single Member I dislike, I have not had an opportunity to meet this new faceless mass, these new Conservatives. I cannot judge them because no one gets up to speak. No one says anything. Perhaps they are still in awe of this Chamber or in awe of you, Mr. Speaker. I know that you gave these new Members indoctrination lessons to the House of Commons. It is a privilege to be elected here, and the greatest honour for any citizen is to receive the tribute of being elected by one's peers to the House of Commons of Canada.
We are proud of that and we have exercised our rights. I call on Conservative Members to retrieve their dignity and their independence as Members. Show your constituents that you are not nameless, faceless and anonymous cyphers sitting in the House of Commons. Their constituents elected them, yet there have only been 3.2 hours of debate in 14 speeches.
The people have spoken. Why don't you listen?

The people have spoken but they expect you to speak. The people of London wanted you to speak. You ought to get up.
We do not have a government by referendum or a government by plebiscite whereby the citizens of this country would be expected to vote on every piece of legislation. They elect each one of us to cast our best judgment, use our best experience and contribute our best eloquence to the consideration of legislation in the House of Commons. Those Conservative Members across the way have been derelict in their duties with respect to this particular piece of legislation.

The Tories have abandoned the principles they said they would uphold. Why closure, Mr. Speaker? I do not think they have any other legislation available.
